newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG prime minister gives way to revolt, steps aside.
newsitem.headline: PNG prime minister gives way to revolt, steps aside.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan said on Wednesday he and two senior ministers would be stepping aside to defuse a 10-day political crisis in the South Pacific nation.

Chan, under fire from army and people over a costly contract with foreign mercenaries, told parliament that he, Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape would stand aside during an inquiry into the mercenary affair.
In an emotional speech to the assembly, he said he would ask cabinet to nominate a caretaker administration.

"Mr Speaker, in the interest and for the good (of the nation) and in order to defuse something that I consider a little bit explosive outside, I will direct the deputy prime minister and the minister for defence to step aside," Chan said.

"I myself will step aside and I will have the cabinet to consider to appoint the acting prime minister," he said, adding that he would leave office for the duration of an inquiry into a controversial mercenary contract.

The news was greeted with a huge roar of approval by thousands of protesters besieging the parliament building to demand Chan's departure over a $36 million contract with the British mercenary company Sandline International.
Around 2,000 protesters cheered madly, lifted soldiers into the air and danced with joy.
Dropping their chants of "Chan resign!" the protesters began to sing the national anthem in the local pidgin language.

The crisis began 10 days ago when army leader Jerry Singirok turned on Chan demanding he quit and expel some 70 African mercenaries hired by Sandline to crush a rebellion and recapture a dormant copper mine on the island of Bougainville.
Singirok was promptly sacked but Chan, a 55-year-old who was serving his second term as prime minister, was unable to control a groundswell of popular and military opposition.
The country was already due to hold national elections in June, but Chan said these might be brought forward "so people can express themselves through the ballot box".
"For those who say I run away, I do not run away," Chan told the parliament.
"To force the prime minister to resign under pressure and duress would be wrong ... that is why I stood firm," he said.
"No government or any parliament should be subject to any pressure," he said.
He criticised the world's media for painting the country in an unflattering light: "They forget we did not fire a shot."
Chan on Tuesday survived a parliamentary vote on an opposition motion calling on him to quit and was to have faced another parliamentary challenge later on Wednesday.
